tur60-0: Teeth Clenching and Grinding (Bruxism): Causes, Effects and Treatment | İhsan Eren
tur60-1: What is teeth clenching and grinding (bruxism), how much force acts on the teeth, and how are the teeth, joint, neck and brain affected? Its links with migraine and fibromyalgia, psychological factors, the place of the night guard, multidisciplinary treatment, botulinum toxin, a short history and six home exercises.
tur60-3: Teeth clenching and grinding (bruxism) is when the chewing muscles work more than they need to, during sleep or during the day. It affects roughly one in four or five people worldwide, and most people do not notice it. Its effects are not limited to the teeth: the jaw joint, neck muscles, sleep and headaches can also be affected. In this guide we explain bruxism from start to finish, like a lesson.

tur60-17: What can you do at home?
tur60-19: About this guide. Our author İhsan Eren learned the approach in this guide from Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation specialist Prof. Dr. Cihan Aksoy (Cihan Hoca), one of the pioneers in Türkiye in the field of jaw joint disorders and teeth clenching, with studies published in international journals since 2005. Cihan Hoca developed an approach that brings dentistry, psychiatry and other specialties together in bruxism and sets out which treatment is medically appropriate in which situation. On this page we include two studies that Cihan Hoca co-authored.
tur60-20: According to the 2018 international consensus, bruxism is chewing-muscle activity that occurs during sleep or while awake, and it has two separate forms. A person can have bruxism without grinding their teeth, simply by clenching or by pushing the lower jaw.
tur60-23: Rhythmic or non-rhythmic activity of the chewing muscles during sleep: grinding and clenching. Most people do not notice it; a bed partner may notice the grinding.
tur60-26: Repeated or sustained tooth contact, clenching, or pushing of the lower jaw while awake. It can happen without your noticing during concentration, stress or intense work.
tur60-28: According to the consensus, in otherwise healthy people bruxism is not a disease in itself but a behaviour; however, it can be a risk factor for consequences such as tooth wear and chewing-muscle and jaw joint pain. Whether bruxism is present is assessed at three levels:
tur60-30: Based only on the person's own report ("I clench my teeth").
tur60-32: There are findings on examination (such as tooth wear or tooth marks on the tongue), with or without the person's own report.
tur60-34: Confirmed by measurement with a device such as a sleep study (polysomnography).
tur60-36: According to a 2024 meta-analysis combining 176 populations, bruxism affects about 22% of people worldwide: sleep bruxism 21%, awake bruxism 23%. In other words, roughly one in four people may clench their teeth during the day. Awake bruxism was reported about twice as often in women as in men (17% vs 8%); no significant difference was found between continents.
tur60-37: How much force acts on the teeth?
tur60-38: Normally the teeth do not touch all day: at rest the lips are closed, the teeth slightly apart and the tongue rests on the roof of the mouth. In clenching, however, the muscles can press the teeth together for hours.
tur60-41: In a study of 10 people, the peak force measured during sleep averaged 42 kilogram-force per person, and the highest value was 81. In some people the night-time force exceeded the strongest bite they could make on purpose during the day (daytime average in the group: 79 kilogram-force).
tur60-44: The strongest human bite on record is 442 kilograms, close to half a tonne; it was measured at a college of dentistry in 1986 and lasted about 2 seconds.
tur60-47: In a study co-authored by Cihan Hoca, maximum bite force and tooth wear were higher in people who clench their teeth, and the relationship between the two was strong. The researchers wrote that this was the first study to show this relationship.
tur60-49: Effects in four areas: teeth, joint, neck, brain
tur60-50: Thinking of teeth clenching only as a dental problem means seeing half the picture. The dashed lines show that the effect can spread like a chain from the jaw to the joint and neck muscles.
tur60-51: Four areas affected by teeth clenching: brain, joint, teeth and neck
tur60-52: Brain: The centre that starts and regulates bruxism; linked to sleep, stress and headache.
tur60-53: Joint: The jaw joint just in front of the ear and the chewing muscles around it.
tur60-54: Teeth: Wear, fractures and cracks; marks on the tongue and cheek.
tur60-55: Neck: Neck muscles that tighten together with clenching.
tur60-57: Bruxism is now regarded as a behaviour mainly regulated by the brain; the bite and the structure of the jaw play only a small role. In a study of patients with sleep bruxism, in 79% of clenching episodes an arousal-like increase in brain waves was seen about 4 seconds before the muscle activity, with an acceleration of heart rate just before it. In other words, clenching during sleep often appears together with a brief lightening of sleep (micro-arousal). Complaints associated with teeth grinding also include disrupted sleep (yours or your bed partner's) and headache. Snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep (sleep apnoea) have also been found to be associated with bruxism.
tur60-58: 2. Joint: the jaw joint and the chewing muscles
tur60-59: Chewing muscles that are clenched for long periods tire and ache; pain in the jaw joint, limited mouth opening and a clicking sound can occur. According to the international headache classification, after tooth pain, jaw joint problems are the most common cause of facial pain. A painless click is common and does not need treatment on its own; if there is pain, locking or limited mouth opening, an assessment is needed. For more detail, see the jaw joint disorders guide.
tur60-60: 3. Teeth: wear, fractures and marks inside the mouth
tur60-61: Clenching and grinding can lead to tooth wear, sensitivity to hot and cold, broken fillings and teeth, cracks in the teeth and problems with dentures. There are clues inside the mouth too: in a 2026 study of 98 patients in Türkiye, among those with bruxism confirmed by a sleep study, 65.3% had tooth marks on the edges of the tongue and 75.5% had a white line on the inside of the cheek along the level of the teeth. The dentist examines tooth wear and the bite (occlusion); however, the bite is no longer seen as the main cause of bruxism.
tur60-63: It is not only the jaw muscles that work when you clench: in a muscle activity study in healthy people, the activity of the front neck muscles rose markedly during maximum clenching. Jaw joint problems are also more common in people with neck pain: in a 2026 meta-analysis that reviewed nine studies, people with neck pain were about 3.6 times more likely to have a jaw joint problem (very low certainty evidence).
tur60-64: Many people turn to one treatment after another for complaints such as waking up tired, morning headaches, and neck and shoulder pain; in clinic I see that teeth clenching can sometimes turn out to be behind these complaints. In advanced cases that do not settle, I also come across pain that spreads from the neck to the arm and resembles nerve root compression but is not true root compression. You can read what nerve root compression is in the cervical disc herniation guide. I share this as my own observation, not as a research finding; not everyone may respond in the same way.
tur60-65: Can be seen alongside migraine, fibromyalgia and neck pain
tur60-66: Jaw joint and chewing-muscle problems often occur together with other diagnoses, and their symptoms can overlap. For this reason, in someone being assessed for headache, widespread body pain or neck pain, the jaw joint and chewing muscles should also be examined.
tur60-69: The classification has a separate heading: headache attributed to a jaw joint disorder. It is usually in the temples and gets worse with chewing and clenching; it can be confused with tension-type headache. In one meta-analysis, people with migraine were 4–5 times more likely to have a jaw joint problem (low to very low certainty evidence).
tur60-71: In a meta-analysis combining 19 studies, 76.8% of people with fibromyalgia had a jaw joint problem; about a third (32.7%) of those with a jaw joint problem also had fibromyalgia.
tur60-73: People with neck pain were about 3.6 times more likely to have a jaw joint problem (very low certainty evidence). The authors recommend assessing the neck and jaw together.
tur60-75: Why does it happen? Psychological and other factors
tur60-76: Bruxism has no single cause; several factors play a part together. It used to be thought that problems with how the teeth meet were the main cause; today these factors are accepted as playing a small role, and bruxism is regarded as mainly regulated by the brain.
tur60-78: The most commonly cited factors. In one systematic review, people with stress were about twice as likely to have bruxism (low certainty evidence).
tur60-80: Snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep (sleep apnoea) are associated with bruxism.
tur60-81: It can appear as a side effect of some medicines; do not stop your medicine on your own, talk to your physician.
tur60-83: Alcohol, smoking, some recreational drugs and six or more cups of caffeinated drinks (tea, coffee) a day can increase the risk.
tur60-84: Psychological factors: why do they matter?
tur60-85: In a study co-authored by Cihan Hoca that examined 273 patients attending a multidisciplinary jaw joint clinic, being female, insufficient social support and muscle-related facial pain increased the likelihood of anxiety or depression. The authors recommended that anxiety and depression be considered alongside muscle and joint problems when planning treatment. For coping with stress, see the what can you do in stressful moments? page.
tur60-86: Night guard: protects the teeth, does not solve the problem
tur60-87: A night guard (mouth guard) is an appliance made by a dentist and usually worn at night. By keeping the teeth apart it helps prevent wear and can reduce the clenching sensation and pain. However, a night guard has not been shown to reduce the clenching behaviour.
tur60-90: A night guard may protect the teeth against wear.
tur60-93: There is not enough evidence that a night guard reduces sleep bruxism; in reviews, night guards did not show effectiveness in the short term.
tur60-95: Because clenching may continue, the load on the muscles and joint can persist; so a night guard is used together with other approaches.
tur60-96: The dentist assesses tooth wear, fractures and cracks, and how the teeth meet (occlusion), and decides whether a night guard is needed and which type.
tur60-98: At present no treatment anywhere in the world has been shown to eliminate teeth clenching for good. In reviews, night guards, biofeedback and botulinum toxin did not show definite effectiveness in the short term; although some medicines reduced clenching episodes during sleep, caution is needed because of side effects, and the reliability of these reviews is very low. So the aim is to protect the teeth, joint and muscles, reduce the triggers and ease the symptoms. This often requires several specialties to work together.
tur60-101: Assessment of wear, fractures and the bite; a night guard if needed.
tur60-103: Assessment and treatment if there is anxiety, depression or intense stress; methods such as cognitive behavioural therapy.
tur60-106: If sleep apnoea is suspected, assessment by a physician and a sleep study if needed.
tur60-108: Awareness and habit change, relaxation, jaw and neck exercises, muscle massage, posture. In a review of 24 studies, muscle pain and activity, mouth opening, anxiety and stress could improve; however, the quality of the evidence was very low.
tur60-109: Only with a specialist physician's prescription
tur60-110: Limited evidence: a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence in seven small studies. In a study of 20 people, gabapentin reduced night-time muscle activity as much as a night guard; the only publication we could include for pregabalin, from the same group, is a single-patient case report. Do not use them on your own; ask your physician which one is suitable.
tur60-113: Injected into the chewing and temple muscles. In a 2025 review of 14 reviews, a reduction in pain was reported in 10, in clenching episodes in 7 and in bite force in 5; however, the reliability of all of them was low or critically low, and no firm conclusion could be drawn.
tur60-114: Which muscles is botulinum toxin injected into?
tur60-115: The schematic drawing below shows the two muscles used for botulinum toxin injections in teeth clenching. The dots are only to show the area; the physician decides the actual injection points and dose.
tur60-116: Temple muscle and chewing muscle: the muscles used for botulinum toxin injections (schematic)
tur60-117: Temple muscle (temporalis): Fans out over the temple, above the ear; it closes the jaw and clenches the teeth.
tur60-118: Chewing muscle (masseter): Runs from the cheekbone to the corner of the lower jaw; you can feel it harden in your cheek when you clench your teeth.
tur60-120: Lips closed, teeth slightly apart, tongue on the roof of the mouth. Whenever you notice you are clenching during the day, return to this position.
tur60-122: To notice clenching during moments of concentration or worry, you can set a phone reminder or put a small note on your desk; the first step in changing a habit is noticing it.
tur60-124: Do not chew gum; avoid biting your nails, lips, tongue or gums, and do not chew pens; support your jaw with your hand when you yawn.
tur60-126: Applying warmth to sore muscles for 10–15 minutes or ice massage for 5–10 minutes can bring relief.
tur60-128: Regular sleep times; cutting down on caffeine, alcohol and smoking, especially in the evening. Tips for sleep are on the sleep page.
tur60-129: Slow breathing, regular exercise and mindfulness practice can reduce how much stress shows up in the muscles.
tur60-130: Do the movements slowly, within a pain-free range. If the pain increases, stop and talk to a physiotherapist or physician.
tur60-131: Sit comfortably; relax your shoulders and jaw, and keep your teeth from touching. Breathe in calmly through your nose and breathe out slowly. As you breathe out, feel the muscles on both sides of your face and your temples soften.
tur60-133: Teeth grinding can also occur in children. It usually appears after the baby teeth or adult teeth first come through and usually stops once the adult teeth have fully developed. If you are concerned, especially if it is affecting your child's sleep, see a physician; if there is tooth wear or pain, a dentist can also assess it.
tur60-134: From the Psalms to international consensus
tur60-135: Teeth grinding has been known since ancient times. It was given a name in the 20th century; for many years the bite was considered the main cause. In the last 25 years, however, it has become clear that bruxism is a behaviour mainly regulated by the brain.
tur60-137: Teeth grinding is also mentioned in several verses of the Psalms.
tur60-139: Viennese dentist Karolyi described clenching and grinding as "traumatic neuralgia".
tur60-140: Marie and Pietkiewicz proposed a French term for teeth grinding.
tur60-141: Frohman coined the term "bruxism", derived from Greek words meaning "to grind the teeth".
tur60-143: The idea that problems with how the teeth meet (occlusion) were the main cause came to the fore; research and treatment focused on bite adjustments and night guards.
tur60-144: It was shown that before clenching during sleep there is an arousal-like increase in brain waves and an acceleration of heart rate (J Dent Res). In the same year it was written that bruxism is mainly regulated by the brain, with the bite playing only a small role.
tur60-145: Cochrane review: there is not enough evidence that a night guard reduces sleep bruxism; a night guard may protect the teeth against wear.
tur60-146: Study co-authored by Cihan Hoca (Arch Oral Biol): in people who clench their teeth, maximum bite force and tooth wear were higher and strongly related to each other; the researchers wrote that this was the first study to show this relationship.
tur60-147: International experts agreed on a common definition of bruxism.
tur60-148: International consensus: two separate definitions for sleep and awake bruxism; in healthy people not a disease but a behaviour that can have consequences.
tur60-149: Meta-analysis combining 176 populations (J Clin Med): worldwide, sleep bruxism about 21%, awake bruxism 23%.
tur60-150: Will my clenching stop if I wear a night guard?
tur60-151: Usually not. A Cochrane review of five studies did not find enough evidence that a night guard reduces sleep bruxism; a night guard may mainly protect the teeth against wear. Because clenching may continue, the load on the muscles and joint can persist. So a night guard is considered not on its own but together with stress management, changing habits and muscle work. Your dentist decides the type of night guard and when to wear it.
tur60-152: I have tooth marks on the edges of my tongue; does it mean I clench my teeth?
tur60-153: It may. In a 2026 study of 98 patients in Türkiye, 65.3% of those with bruxism confirmed by a sleep study had tooth marks on the edges of the tongue, compared with 34.7% of those who only reported clenching themselves. A white line on the inside of the cheek along the level of the teeth was seen in 75.5% and 42.9% respectively. These signs do not make a diagnosis on their own; they are assessed together with a dental examination.
tur60-154: My jaw clicks; is it related to clenching?
tur60-155: A click may be related to the disc inside the jaw joint shifting as the mouth opens and closes. A painless click is common and does not need treatment on its own. If the sound comes with pain, limited mouth opening or catching, it should be assessed. Clenching can be a risk factor for chewing-muscle and jaw joint pain; for more detail, see the jaw joint disorders guide.
tur60-157: Stress and anxiety are among the most commonly cited factors. In a systematic review of six studies (three in the meta-analysis), people with stress were about twice as likely to have bruxism (OR 2.07); however, the certainty of the evidence was low. In a study co-authored by Cihan Hoca that examined 273 patients attending a jaw joint clinic, being female, insufficient social support and muscle-related facial pain increased the likelihood of anxiety or depression; the authors recommended that anxiety and depression be considered when planning treatment.
tur60-158: Does a botulinum toxin injection treat teeth clenching?
tur60-159: Botulinum toxin is an injection given only by physicians, and for clenching it is injected into the chewing and temple muscles. In a 2025 overview of 14 systematic reviews, a reduction in pain was reported in 10, in clenching episodes in 7 and in maximum bite force in 5. However, the reliability of all the reviews was low or critically low, and no firm conclusion could be drawn. Your physician decides whether it is suitable.
tur60-160: Do I need medicine for teeth clenching?
tur60-161: Most people do not. A Cochrane review of medicines for sleep bruxism did not find enough evidence in seven small studies that medicines are effective; side effects were seen with some medicines. Gabapentin, a medicine used for nerve pain, reduced night-time chewing-muscle activity as much as a night guard in a small study of 20 people. The only publication we could include for pregabalin, from the same group of medicines as gabapentin, is a case report of a single patient with an anxiety disorder who clenched during the day. These medicines are used only with a specialist physician's prescription and supervision; do not use them on your own. Ask your physician which one is suitable.

tur60-163: Does teeth clenching go away completely?
tur60-164: At present no treatment anywhere in the world has been shown to eliminate teeth clenching for good. In reviews, night guards, biofeedback and botulinum toxin did not show definite effectiveness in the short term; although some medicines reduced clenching episodes during sleep, caution is needed because of side effects, and the reliability of these reviews is very low. Because bruxism is a behaviour mainly regulated by the brain, the aim is to protect the teeth, joint and muscles, reduce the triggers and ease the symptoms. This often requires several specialties to work together.
tur60-165: See a physician or dentist in the following situations; how urgent each is, is shown at the start of each group.
tur60-166: Jaw pain together with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating
tur60-167: Sudden numbness or weakness in the face, or difficulty speaking
tur60-168: See a physician or dentist the same day:

tur60-170: Swelling of the face or jaw together with a fever
tur60-171: Over the age of 50, new temple pain, jaw pain when chewing or talking, or problems with vision
